title: A 100 km and 30 day neighbor filter cut annual count dispersion beyond random thinning for shallow M5.5+ earthquakes in 2001-2025
abstract: We tested whether removal of events with a recent nearby predecessor reduces annual count dispersion more than uniform random removal. We used a fixed USGS ComCat snapshot, shallow events at preferred magnitude 5.5 or more, year 2000 for filter history and 2001-2025 for scoring. A 100 km and 30 day filter retained 6,629 of 10,051 events. Annual variance divided by mean fell from 11.84 to 2.26. Equal-size random subsets gave a central 95% range of 6.81 to 9.56. No value in 19,999 draws was as low as the filter value. Planned window, magnitude, reverse-time and linear-trend checks gave the same direction. The reverse-time result limits causal interpretation. The test shows that local concentration is linked to annual variance beyond count loss alone. It does not identify a physical aftershock fraction, prove global independence or test a Poisson process. One catalog, fixed windows, 25 scored years and conditional reference distributions limit inference. Code, provenance, aggregate results, all simulation statistics, an independent audit and a figure are included. Source records stay external.

display.caption: Annual counts before and after the primary neighbor filter, and dispersion under seven filters versus equal-size random removal. Bars give central 95% conditional reference ranges, not physical confidence intervals.
